after.label: Strategic & military scholarship
after.description: Brings strategic reasoning, critical campaign scholarship and the editing of military texts into view. Clausewitz, Jomini, Delbrück, Mahan, Corbett and the translated Sun Tzu tradition pose different questions about judgment, evidence and the purposes of war. Professional education and academic inquiry overlap without being identical.

after.scope_note: A selective teaching umbrella, weighted toward European and Anglophone scholarship, with a Chinese text and its mediated reception distinguished. Delbrück explicitly uses Ranke, Beloch and biographical research; these roots are not independent of every other historical tradition. Theory does not guarantee successful action. Marie’s editing and later translations are substantive mediation. Corbett writes for an imperial setting; neither that perspective nor Mahan’s national judgments is universalized. Bassford’s later online corrections are not assigned to his 1994 argument.

strands.title: Strategic principles, uncertainty and judgment
strands.focus: Clausewitz’s friction and variable tendencies and Jomini’s qualified rules frame different questions. Neither makes war wholly mechanical.
strands.works: On War (1832), selections; The Art of War (1862 translation), conclusion

strands.title: Editing and translating strategic texts

strands.title: Chinese strategic writing and its translation

strands.works: The Art of War, Giles translation (1910), preface and III §§1–8

strands.title: Documents and practical possibility

strands.title: Sea power and maritime coordination

strands.title: Culture, politics and disputed reception

after.scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück and strategic scholarship supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production.

strands.title: Finance, bargaining and geographic scope

before.label: Historical demography & history of the family
before.description: Combines related inquiries into population, households, childhood and intimate relations. Henry’s family reconstitution and Cambridge’s aggregate and household studies differ from Ariès’s historical concepts and Stone’s family interpretation. Pollock’s criticism questions evidence and sweeping changes in parental care. Lee and Wang’s Chinese population study challenges received Malthusian comparisons without making the field’s regional patterns uniform.

Additional selections: Hajnal (1965); Laslett and Wall (1972); Pollock (1981/1983); Wrigley, Davies, Oeppen and Schofield (1997); Lee and Wang (1999).

added.relationship: Completing Pertz’s Gneisenau biography becomes a route into Delbrück’s wider military scholarship

added.relationship: Keegan challenges Clausewitz through an account that places culture against political explanation

wartradition.internal_distinctions: Six approaches distinguish principles/judgment, editing/translation, Chinese text reception, critical historical method, maritime coordination and the culture/politics debate. Delbrück combines philological and practical criticism rather than inventing a separate all-purpose method. Jomini admits uncertainty; Clausewitz is not wholly rational control. Chinese attribution and reception are not a uniform Asian tradition, and British imperial purposes remain situated.

Add Howard/Paret’s translation as interpretation and Keegan’s specific critique, the latter mediated by Bassford. These have named mechanisms and preserve the difference between historical resources, later reception and a school’s founding.

Add Bassford’s directed criticism of Keegan without treating all strategic scholarship as his position. No Sun Tzu-to-Clausewitz or Mahan-to-Corbett transmission is inferred from juxtaposition; the broad group roster does not create personal influence arrows.
wartradition.evidence_and_interpretation: Source notes distinguish authorial text, translator/editor apparatus, self-reported intellectual debts, mediated original passages and retrospective criticism. Marie’s modest disclaimer does not erase her work; Maude’s editorial footnote is not Clausewitz. Bassford’s post-2000 web corrections are not dated 1994. Giles’s translation judgments and Sutton’s digital losses are disclosed. Delbrück’s political limits and differing terrain assessments remain attributed.

Keegan’s restricted battle frame and the European weighting of the military-revolution debate prevent a claim to global comprehensiveness.

Thompson essay remains mediated by Rogers.
